evidence.label: Bounded-degree coboundary expanders in every dimension

headline: Large higher-dimensional expanders with a bounded number of faces at each point exist in every dimension.
scope: The paper builds complexes in every dimension of at least 3, with coefficients 0 and 1. The one- and two-dimensional cases come from earlier work. Constants may depend on the dimension.
plain: An expander is a network with no bottlenecks, even when very large. Coboundary expanders are the higher-dimensional version, built from triangles, tetrahedra and beyond. This paper builds them for every dimension from 3 up, with a bounded number of faces at each point. With earlier cases, they now exist in every dimension.
doesNot: This does not give explicit values for the degree bound or the expansion constant.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mikhail Gromov, who asked for bounded-degree complexes with uniform filling bounds
scorecard.significanceWhy: It completes the existence question for bounded-degree coboundary expanders, a central object in high-dimensional expansion.

explanation:
Put ten points around a ring and join each point to its two neighbors. Pick five points in a row. Only two links leave that group, so the ratio is 2 to 5, or 0.4. Take a ring of a thousand points and pick half of them in a row. Still only two links leave, and the ratio falls to 0.004. A large ring has a bottleneck.

The Petersen graph does much better. It has ten points, each joined to three others. Check every group of at most five points. At least as many links leave the group as there are points in it. The worst ratio is exactly 1. Networks that keep such a ratio above a fixed number, as they grow, are called expanders. In an expander, the links leaving a group measure how far the group is from nothing or everything[1].

Coboundary expansion carries this idea to higher dimensions. Build a shape from points, links, filled triangles, filled tetrahedra and so on. Such a shape is a simplicial complex, and its pieces are called faces. Choose a set of links. Its coboundary is the set of triangles that contain an odd number of the chosen links[2]. Some sets of links have an empty coboundary for a trivial reason: they come from a set of points. Take all links leaving some group of points, and every triangle contains zero or two of them. A complex is a coboundary expander when the converse holds in a strong, measured form. A small coboundary forces the set to be close to one of those trivial sets. The same must hold one level up, two levels up, and so on.

There is a catch. Some complexes have holes, like the hollow inside a doughnut. A hole gives a set whose coboundary is empty, yet it is not close to any trivial set. So coboundary expansion also demands that the complex have no such holes, at every level below the top[3].

Mikhail Gromov asked in 2010 for large complexes of this kind with a bounded number of faces at each point[4]. In 2019, Lubotzky, Luria and Rosenthal built random expanders in every dimension[5]. But in their complexes, the number of faces at each point grows with the size[6]. Evra and Kaufman got bounded-degree complexes in every dimension with a weaker property that allows holes[7]. Chapman and Lubotzky settled the two-dimensional case in 2025[8]. Other work did not give the needed absence of holes at every level[9].

This paper proves the remaining case: every dimension from 3 up[10]. For each such dimension d, it builds a family of ever larger d-dimensional complexes. Every point lies in at most a fixed number of top faces. The expansion constant is the same for every member of the family, at every level below d[11]. Together with graphs and the two-dimensional case, this gives such expanders in every dimension.

The obstacle was proving there are no holes. A weaker measured inequality was already known for this family of complexes. It measures distance only to sets with empty coboundary, so it tolerates holes. The family comes from matrix groups built from polynomials. Small fixed groups describe the neighborhood of each point, which keeps the number of faces bounded[12]. The new work shows that every finite member of the family has no holes below the top level. That lets the earlier inequality be upgraded into full coboundary expansion[13].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the construction for every dimension of at least 3. The graph and two-dimensional cases, used to cover every dimension, are separate results. The constants may depend on the dimension. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proof holds. Lean has checked a formal version of the construction in dimensions 3 and up. The lower-dimensional cases are earlier results, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A network where every group of points, up to half of them, has many links leaving it, compared with its size.
A shape built from points, links, filled triangles, filled tetrahedra and higher versions.
One of the pieces of a simplicial complex: a point, link, triangle, tetrahedron and so on.
For a set of faces, the faces one level up that contain an odd number of them.
Here, a set of faces with empty coboundary that does not come from a lower level; it signals nonzero cohomology.
A computer program that checks each step of a formally written proof.
